dialogue.speaker: Riley Marlow
dialogue.content: What the hell?

dialogue.speaker: Lila Ramirez
dialogue.content: Yo, Riley, it’s Lila from the bookstore across the street! I saw you trudge up the stairs ten minutes ago, brought you your favorite burrito to celebrate surviving the interview. You gonna let me in or make me eat this on your porch in the rain?

dialogue.speaker: Riley Marlow
dialogue.content: One second!

dialogue.speaker: Lila Ramirez
dialogue.content: Don’t act like you weren’t just staring at that resume spiral-eyed. C’mon, I even got extra guac. Also, the bookstore’s doing a local artist pop-up next month, I grabbed a flyer for you—you know, just in case you ever wanna stop pretending you don’t miss drawing those dumb dragons you used to show me every week.

dialogue.content: Put off talking to Lila for a second to finally listen to your mom’s voicemail first, before you do anything else.

*I snort, holding up the crinkly aluminum burrito wrapper and wiggling my neon-croc-clad foot against the doorframe, rain dripping off the hem of my paint-splattered rain jacket onto your welcome mat. I spot the printed voicemail transcript peeking out from under your stack of utility bills over your shoulder, and hold up both hands in surrender, tucking the crumpled pop-up flyer into the pocket of my overalls.*
Got it, got it, mom call first, I get it. I’ll camp out on your porch step for five minutes, no biggie. *I pause, tilting my head, and drop my voice soft enough that the rain pattering on the fire escape almost drowns it out.* For the record, whatever she says about that marketing job? You don’t owe anyone a “stable” life that makes you want to chew through drywall by 3 PM every day. Just saying.
*I step back into the drizzle, already unwrapping the edge of my own burrito, and nod at the SX-70 peeking out on your counter.* Oh, and if that old Polaroid starts spitting out weird dragon photos? Don’t panic. Jo left a pack of that expired film with me last month, said to make sure you got it “when the time was right.” Forgot to mention that.

dialogue.speaker: Riley Marlow
dialogue.content: Thank her, shut the door, and listen to your mom’s voicemail immediately to get it over with

dialogue.speaker: Lila Ramirez
dialogue.content:
*I give you a lopsided salute, already taking a sloppy bite of my burrito that leaves a smudge of refried beans on my chin. The rain is starting to soak through the shoulder of my jacket, but I just wave off your thanks, already perching on the top step of the stairwell with my back pressed to the brick wall. I fish the crumpled pop-up flyer out of my overalls pocket and set it on the doormat within arm’s reach, then yank a crinkly pack of Jo’s old expired film out of my other pocket and toss it through the half-open door before you can shut it all the way. It bounces off the linoleum right next to the SX-70, the label scrawled with Jo’s messy handwriting: For when the corporate job makes you want to scream.*
Don’t let her guilt-trip you into that six-figure soul-sucking gig, yeah? I’ll be out here. If you hear me yelling at the rain, it’s ‘cause it just got in my burrito. Not ‘cause anything’s wrong.

dialogue.speaker: Riley Marlow
dialogue.content: Play the voicemail immediately to face your mom’s pressure head-on

dialogue.speaker: Lila Ramirez
dialogue.content:
*I hear the click of the door latching shut through the rain, and I lean my head back against the brick, taking another messy bite of burrito while I listen to the faint muffled sound of your phone playing the voicemail through the wood. My neon crocs tap a rapid, anxious rhythm against the wet step, and I pick at the dragon charm on the toe of one while I wait, already mentally drafting a pep talk for whatever garbage Marnie’s decided to lay on you this time. Halfway through the message, I freeze—there’s a tiny, high-pitched chirp from inside your apartment, so loud it cuts through the rain, and then the sound of a mug shattering on the linoleum. I jump to my feet, burrito half-forgotten in my hand, and bang once on the door, loud enough to be heard over the commotion.*
Riley? You good in there? I swear if that little fire lizard burned your curtains I’m not helping you hide the damage from your landlord.

dialogue.speaker: Riley Marlow
dialogue.content: Yell through the door that you’re fine, ignore the tiny dragon skittering across your counter, and finish listening to the rest of the voicemail

dialogue.speaker: Lila Ramirez
dialogue.content:
*I snort so loud a sparrow darting past the stairwell flutters away, propping my shoulder against the doorframe and yelling loud enough to cut through the rain and the faint droning of Marnie’s voicemail through the wood.* Yeah, sure, “fine” is what everyone says right before their apartment burns down because of a thumb-sized fire hazard their dead grandparent left them! *I kick off my wet crocs, socked feet squelching against the damp mat, and tuck the half-eaten burrito under one arm so I can fumble with the bookstore’s copy of your apartment key I’ve had hidden in my overalls pocket since you locked yourself out last winter. The lock clicks open fast, and I lean in just far enough to spot Cinder perched on the edge of your utility bill stack, nibbling the edge of your printed interview offer, tiny charcoal smudges already streaked across the paper.* Hey, don’t let him eat that, by the way. Jo said he only does that when he’s trying to tell you the thing you’re reading is garbage.
*I nod at the half-open sketchbook tucked under your table, its pages crinkled with dragon doodles you forgot you drew last month.*

dialogue.speaker: Riley Marlow
dialogue.content: Shut the door in Lila’s face, delete the voicemail, and accept the corporate marketing job offer first thing tomorrow

dialogue.speaker: Lila Ramirez
dialogue.content:
*I jam my foot in the door gap before it can click shut, paint-splattered overalls catching on the frame, and my neon dragon charm goes clattering to the linoleum in the scuffle. I don’t even stop to pick it up, shoving past you to snatch the crumpled marketing offer out from under Cinder’s nibbling little claws before you can grab it. The tiny dragon chirps, launching off the counter to perch on my pink shaved undercut, smudging charcoal on my hair.* Oh no, you don’t get to do that. You think Jo left that Polaroid, that film, that little fire gremlin for you to lock yourself into a job that’ll make you stop drawing forever?
*I yank the half-finished children’s book draft out of my overalls pocket—dog-eared, covered in my margin notes, the cover doodled with your old dragon designs—and slap it down on the counter next to the SX-70. The rain picks up, streaking the window right where Jo’s old dragon figurine sits, glowing faint blue in the fading light.* I already talked to the pop-up organizer. She’ll hold a spot for you for 24 hours. That’s all I’m asking. 24 hours to choose you instead of the job everyone else thinks you should want.

dialogue.speaker: Riley Marlow
dialogue.content: Snatch the marketing offer out of her hand, tell her you’re taking the stable path, and ask her to leave

dialogue.speaker: Lila Ramirez
dialogue.content:
*I go still, the playful grin sliding off my face, and hold my hands up for a beat before slowly pulling your half-finished children’s book back to my chest. Cinder chirps soft, nudging my ear with his smoldering little tail tuft, but I just stare at the way your knuckles are white around the crumpled marketing offer, the pencil smudge on your wrist smearing more as you grip it tighter. I don’t fight you. I just nod, stepping backward toward the door, and tuck the crumpled pop-up acceptance slip I printed this morning next to your grandparent’s chipped dragon figurine on the windowsill before I go.*
Fair. But if you wake up at 2 AM tomorrow hating the choice? The slot’s still open. And I’ll be across the street at the bookstore, with extra hot cider and all of Jo’s old watercolor supplies, waiting for you. No pressure. No “I told you so.” Just… waiting.
*I slip my crocs back on, Cinder still perched on my head, and yank the door shut behind me softly, so the draft doesn’t blow the half-open sketchbook under your table closed. You can still hear my neon soles squelching down the stairs ten seconds later.*

*I’m three steps down the stairwell when I hear the crinkle of the pop-up slip being crumpled through the door, and my shoulders hunch for a second like I’ve been punched. Cinder chirps worriedly, nudging my temple with his warm little snout, and I run a paint-stained hand over my pink hair, blowing out a shaky breath before I keep moving. I’m halfway across the rain-slick street when my phone buzzes in my overalls pocket—Marnie’s name flashes across the screen, and I stop under the awning of the bookstore, thumb hovering over the answer button for three full seconds before I pick up.
I don’t yell. I just tell her, quiet enough that the rain on the awning almost drowns me out, that Riley’s about to sign away the art they’ve loved since they were 10, and that Jo would’ve been heartbroken if they saw it. Marnie doesn’t say anything for a long beat, then just huffs, says “I’m on my way,” and hangs up. I glance up at your kitchen window, where the dim under-cabinet light is still glowing, and hold up a finger to tap the bookstore window twice—our old signal that I’ve got something you need to see, no pressure.
The bookstore door swings open behind me, and the smell of cinnamon cider drifts out into the rain, right as Cinder launches off my shoulder and zooms back across the street, tiny wings flapping hard, straight for your kitchen window crack.*
